turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been miserable since the middle of the night. I finally got him in the car.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah and the parking garage was a nightmare, some guy in a truck took two spots. Anyway. My side is killing me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): I'll get you set up. Doctor'll be right in. You want a blanket?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, sure, I'm kinda chilly actually. Tell him it's the left side, it goes right down into my groin.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Morning. I already caught left side down to the groin. Walk me through last night in your own words.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was fine at dinner, we had leftover chili, which, not important. Then around two, maybe 2:30, I woke up with this pain in my left loin, like someone wringing it, and it shot down toward my groin.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): And I threw up once, just the once, around three. There was blood in my pee this morning, pink and then darker.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. When it grabs you, if ten is the worst pain you have ever had, where are you sitting?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, maybe an eight? Or a nine when it clamps down. I don't know, it's bad. I can't get comfortable.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was pacing the hallway. Wouldn't sit, wouldn't eat the eggs I made.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I couldn't look at food. Still a bit queasy, but I haven't thrown up again.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any burning when you pass urine, or going more often?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning. Not going more often. It stings a little from the pain, well, actually no, it doesn't burn.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any diarrhea, or pain across the lower belly like a stomach bug?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No diarrhea. The pain stays in the left loin and groin, not really the middle.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath, chest pain, cough?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of that. Breathing's fine.
[SEG0018] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He felt hot in the car. I thought he was just worked up.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I had some chills, yeah. Not sure if that's a fever or just the pain.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me feel your belly while we talk. Soft. Tender right over the left flank. No guarding, and I'm not finding rebound.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, yeah that's the spot. This happened sort of once before, last winter, or the one before, I can't pin it down. It faded in a day and I never came in.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. What medicines do you take day to day?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Amloidipine for the pressure, 5 milligrams, every morning. And the cholesterol one at night, twenty milligrams, little white oval, I can never remember the name.

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Sugar tablets, that's metforman for the sugar, five hundred milligrams, one in the morning and one with dinner. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning, a teaspoon, my cousin sends it, I don't know what's actually in it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the ibuprofen.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh right, I stopped the ibuprofen in March. Four hundred milligrams, I was using it when my knee acted up, but my stomach hated it so I quit. And the kidney guy mentioned a water pill, hydrochlorothyazide, but I never took it. Not once.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good, so we won't count a medicine you never started. The pressure, the sugar, the cholesterol, those are ongoing, I'm hearing. When did the sugar tablets start?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Since Diwali or after, I think? My sister's wedding was around then, or maybe the year before, I honestly can't date it. We had so many sweets, which is a whole other story.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies? Penicillin, contrast, anything that swells you up or gives a rash?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. Nothing like that.

[SEG0031] person_3 (NURSE): Vitals while you two talk. Blood pressure is one oh nine over seventy-seven, temperature thirty-eight point three celsius, pulse one oh two, hang on, the clip slipped, it's ninety-six beats a minute. Oxygen ninety-eight percent, weight seventy-two kilograms.
[SEG0032] person_3 (NURSE): For what it's worth, last time in March you were sixty-eight, and your last pressure was one-forty. Today's numbers are the ones I just said.

[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thirty-eight point three is a real fever, and one oh nine over seventy-seven is on the soft side if he used to sit around one-forty. I'm thinking out loud. Pain from the loin into the groin plus blood in the urine is the classic story for a stone dropping down the ureter.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): The fever makes me keep infection on the list, I can't rule that out yet. This still feels more like colic than a straight bladder infection.
[SEG0035] person_3 (NURSE): I dipped the urine before you came in. Large blood, 3 plus. Leukocytes negative. Nitrites negative.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hmm. Blood without the usual infection markers on the dip. That pushes me toward a stone, provisionally, and infection stays a maybe until the labs and the scan.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Is a stone gonna wreck my kidney? My uncle had one and he wouldn't shut up about it for a year. Different uncle from the cousin with the powder. Sorry.

[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Most of these pass, but I don't want to guess the size from the doorway. We'll get a non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis today to look for a stone. And I'll send a CBC and a basic metabolic panel today too.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Today today? I've got the shop to open, and the register does this thing where it jams if you look at it wrong.
[SEG0040] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The shop can wait. Listen to her.

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Today. For the pain, because your stomach didn't like ibuprofen, I'm not reaching for a medicine in that family. We'll give oxycodone, five milligrams by mouth, one dose now. And ondansetron, four milligrams by mouth, one dose now, for the queasiness.
[SEG0042] person_3 (NURSE): I can pull those and give them before the scan. Can he sip water?
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sips of water are fine. I'd like him drinking, not chugging. No food until after the CT, just in case they want him empty.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I have coffee? I usually do two cups, it's basically a personality.

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Skip the coffee today. Water only until the scan is done. If you can't keep fluids down, or the pain jumps past what the oxycodone touches, come straight back to the ER, don't wait on me.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Otherwise I'll see you back in clinic in two days, and we'll go over the CT together.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. Okay. Umm, the powder, should I take that tomorrow morning or leave it?

[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Leave the Ayurvedic powder off until we know what's in it. Keep the amlodipine, the metformin, and the cholesterol pill as you usually do, unless the scan team says otherwise this afternoon.
[SEG0049] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll write that down. Amlodipine in the morning, metformin morning and dinner, cholesterol thing at night. No powder, no coffee.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): My knee's gonna complain without the ibuprofen, but I'm not restarting that, my stomach was a mess. That was March, I'm sure about March. The winter pain I'm not sure about.

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Leave the ibuprofen stopped. The old pain we just can't date, and the sugar start we can't date either, so I won't put a year on those. Anything else hurting that we haven't touched?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I think that's the whole circus. Thanks for not making me feel dumb about the chili.
[SEG0053] person_3 (NURSE): I'll get the oxycodone and the ondansetron, and reception will book the CT for this afternoon and the clinic visit in two days.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. We'll get you more comfortable first, then pictures. Hang in there.

spec.situation: Sudden severe loin pain going to the groin overnight, vomiting once, blood in urine; pain score given loosely; urine dip result read aloud; painkiller and scan planned today.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

omissions.text: Hematuria was described as urine being pink and then darker this morning.
Pain was described as colicky/clamping ('like someone wringing it', 'when it clamps down') and the patient said he could not get comfortable/paced the hallway.
No further vomiting after the single episode; still queasy but has not vomited again.
Fever was not just chills: family member said he felt hot in the car, and doctor interpreted 38.3 C as a real fever.
Urine dipstick details are missing: large blood 3+, leukocytes negative, nitrites negative.
Hydrochlorothiazide was mentioned by a kidney specialist but the patient never started it, not once.
Ibuprofen discontinuation timing was specified as stopped in March because it upset his stomach.
Conditional follow-up was specifically to come straight back to the ER, not just generic follow-up, if unable to keep fluids down or if pain exceeds what oxycodone controls.
The planned clinic follow-up was specifically to review the CT together in two days.
